newsitem.title: CANADA: Weak yen drives up profits at top Japan car firms.
newsitem.headline: Weak yen drives up profits at top Japan car firms.

text.p: Japan's top car makers, Toyota Motor Corp. and Nissan Motor Co. Ltd, reported an impressive surge in profits Friday, thanks to a weaker yen.
The companies said they expected the upward drive in profits in the first six months of Japan's fiscal year to continue through the full year, which ends March 31.

Toyota, Japan's biggest car maker and the world's number two auto company, said its parent current profits for the six months ended Sept. 30 totalled 258.50 billion yen ($2.30 billion), nearly four times as much as it made in the comparable period last year.
"The reason for the rise in the half-year profit is the yen's fall," Toyota Vice Chairman Iwao Isomura told reporters.
Exports were robust, but domestic sales were sluggish, another Toyota official said.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses or gains on non-operating activities, such as investments in stocks.
Toyota said it expects a full-year current profit of 550 billion yen ($4.91 billion) in the current business year, up from 340.73 billion yen ($3.04 billion) a year ago.
Nissan, Japan's second largest car maker, announced it powered out of the red to post a healthy six-month profit.
Its parent current profits were 30.91 billion yen ($275 million), against a parent current loss of 8.8 billion yen ($78.5 million) in the year-earlier period.
It said its operating profit was nearly 7.5 times as big as last year's half-year figure.

"This increase ... was brought on largely by cost reduction and other extensive rationalisation efforts, and foreign exchange profits from the correction in the yen's appreciation," Nissan said in a statement.
The yen stood at about 112 to the dollar Friday, compared with about 100 a year ago.

The cheaper yen makes Japanese products more competitive in overseas markets. Also, when the Japanese currency is weak, companies converting dollar-based overseas earnings into yen get more for their money.
Mitsubishi Motors Corp. also announced its half-year results Friday, but unlike its bigger rivals, it posted a 12.6 percent fall in its parent current profit.
The company said, however, that the figures might have been even worse without the help of the weaker yen.
"We ended with disappointing results as sales in the domestic market in the April-July period were sluggish," Mitsubishi managing director Minoru Wada said.
